827.title: Bridget of Sweden (1303–1373)
827.hook: mother of eight, widow, founder, co-patron of Europe
827.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Bridget's feast in the calendar, and the order she founded, the Bridgettines, still lives and prays in houses in several countries. Some Catholics pray for Europe on her feast and on the feasts of its other patron saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Western Schism: rival popes, and sincere people, saints among them, on different sides. Your line was even saints were confused. Where did you keep going without a clear answer? Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

A fresh grave at a monastery in Sweden. The widow standing beside it was married young. She has raised a houseful of children, run an estate, served at the royal court, and walked a long pilgrimage road beside her husband, Ulf. Now Ulf is buried, and the life she knew is over. The expected next chapter is a quiet one: a chair by the fire, grandchildren, prayers. She is about to do something else. She will begin again, in a new country, with a new work and a voice that reaches popes. Today's word is her name: Bridget.
screen: `A GRAVE IN SWEDEN.` → `A HOUSEFUL OF CHILDREN, NOW GROWN.` → `SHE BEGINS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Start with the first life. Bridget was born into a noble family and married young. Tradition remembers her as a mother who prayed with her children and fed the poor at her own door, and one of her daughters, Catherine, is honored as a saint too. Next, the turn. After Ulf died, Bridget gave away much of what she had and gave herself to prayer. She wrote down visions, later gathered as her Revelations, many of them meditations on the suffering of Christ. The Church is careful here. The Catechism says private revelations don't add to the faith; they can help people live it, and they are weighed, not required. Then, the new work. Bridget founded a religious order, the Order of the Most Holy Savior, under a rule she wrote. And she went to Rome, and she stayed. The popes of her day lived at Avignon, in France, and Bridget, years before Catherine of Siena, wrote to them plainly, urging them to come home to Rome. She did not live to see it settled; yesterday's schism came after her. Finally, Europe. The Church has named Bridget a co-patron of Europe, beside Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein. A woman who crossed the continent on pilgrim roads, from the far north to Rome and on to the Holy Land, now stands for the whole of it. Paul's first letter to Timothy describes a widow who trusts in God and keeps on praying, night and day. Bridget did that, and then she got up and went to work. A second life can be larger than the first.
screen: `A NOBLE WIFE AND MOTHER.` · `WIDOWED, SHE GIVES HERSELF TO PRAYER.` · `AN ORDER FOUNDED, A LIFE IN ROME.` · `A CO-PATRON OF EUROPE.` · then, large: `A WIDOW'S SECOND LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one map. Before the sit, bring to mind the roads Bridget walked, north to south: cold coasts, mountain passes, crowded cities. Or choose one country in Europe you know a little, or have family in. Settle, and breathe slowly. Let a few faces come: a border town, a family that just arrived somewhere new, a parish choir, a teenager on a night train. If you pray, you can ask Bridget's prayers for them, or pray an Our Father with that place in mind. If you don't, just hold it, the way you'd hold a friend's name. The bell holds the time.
Bridget. A noble wife and mother who, once widowed, founded an order, moved to Rome, and spoke plainly to popes. Today's word.

Your line: a widow's second life. Today, notice one person near you who is starting over after a loss, and do one small thing for the new beginning: a call, a meal, a ride. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: The Modern Devotion
828.hook: Dutch lay communities practice simple inner prayer; the Imitation of Christ comes from them
828.howItsDone: Catholics still read The Imitation of Christ, often a chapter or a few lines at a time, and some keep it beside the Bible for daily spiritual reading or use it in retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bridget of Sweden, who buried her husband and began a larger life. Your line was a widow's second life. Whose new beginning did you help along? Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

Nobody in this narrow house in a Dutch town wears a habit. It is late in the middle ages. Nobody has taken vows. The men copy books by hand for a living, pool what they earn, eat at one table, and pray. Down the street, a house of women does much the same, sewing and spinning. On Sunday they all walk to the parish church like their neighbors. What sets them apart is quieter than that. They are trying to let the faith travel from the outside of their lives to the inside. The movement they belonged to came to be called the Modern Devotion. That's today's word.
screen: `NO HABITS, NO VOWS.` → `COPYING, SHARING, PRAYING.` → `FROM THE OUTSIDE TO THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Start with the man tradition puts at the root, Geert Groote, a preacher from Deventer who left a comfortable career and called people back to a plain, interior faith. Around him, laymen and laywomen began living together as the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life, and others became canons in religious houses linked to the movement. Next, the method. Their prayer was simple. Read a little Scripture, slowly. Copy out a line that strikes you, keep it close, and return to it through the day. Look honestly at your own heart at night. No ladders of mystical stages. Just an ordinary day, turned toward God. Then, the book. From these communities came The Imitation of Christ, which tradition attributes to Thomas à Kempis, a canon of one of their houses. It opens with Jesus's words from John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." And then it turns inward again and again. Early on it says, in effect, that a humble knowledge of yourself is a surer road to God than deep learning. Finally, the direction: inward. In Luke, Jesus says, "the kingdom of God is within you." The Modern Devotion took him at his word. Not instead of the Mass and the sacraments; they kept those. Underneath them. The outward life mattered. The Devotion kept asking what was going on inside it. Copyists, weavers, schoolmasters, with ordinary jobs, doing one quiet thing on purpose every day.
screen: `GEERT GROOTE AND THE COMMON LIFE.` · `READ A LITTLE, SLOWLY. KEEP ONE LINE.` · `THE IMITATION OF CHRIST.` · `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.` · then, large: `INWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray simply. Choose one short line. Today's will do: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness. Or any line of Scripture or poetry you already keep. Settle, and say it once, slowly, in your head. Then stay with it. When your mind drifts to the dishes or the inbox, don't scold it. Come back to the line, plainly, the way you'd turn back to a friend after a car horn in the street. If you pray, let the line become your prayer. If you don't, let it be a place to rest. The bell holds the time.
Modern Devotion. Lay communities in the Low Countries who practiced plain, inward prayer, and from whom The Imitation of Christ came. Today's word.
Your line: inward. Today, write one line from something you read on a scrap of paper, keep it in your pocket, and read it again once before the day ends. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: Joan's trial
829.hook: the transcripts survive: asked if she was in God's grace, she answered carefully and wisely
829.howItsDone: Catholics honor Joan of Arc as a saint and one of the patron saints of France, and her trial records are still read and studied; some keep her feast with Mass and with prayers for France.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Modern Devotion, ordinary people praying plainly and turning the faith inward. Your line was inward. What line did you carry in your pocket? Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

Do you know if you are in the grace of God? The question comes across a room full of churchmen in Rouen. The young woman on the bench is a prisoner, a peasant girl who led soldiers and is now on trial for her life. The trap is plain to see. If she says yes, she claims to know what only God knows. If she says no, she has just confessed. There is no safe answer. Her reply was taken down by the court's own notaries, and the record still survives. Today is Joan's trial.
screen: `ARE YOU IN THE GRACE OF GOD?` → `YES IS PRESUMPTION.` → `NO IS A CONFESSION.`

segments.voice: Start with who she was. Joan of Arc was a peasant girl who said the voices of saints had told her to help the French king. She went to war, she was captured, and she was handed to a church court sitting in a city under English rule. The charge was heresy. The stakes were political too. Next, the question. Catholic teaching, as the Council of Trent later put it, holds that no one can be certain, by their own reckoning, of being in God's grace. So the question had only bad answers, and it was asked to catch her. Then, her answer. As the record gives it, she said: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so. Notice what she did. She didn't claim certainty. She didn't confess guilt. She turned the question into a prayer and handed the answer back to God. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his disciples that when they are handed over they should "take no thought how or what to speak," because it will be given them in that hour. Some readers hear Joan's reply as exactly that. Finally, how it ended. The court condemned her, and she was burned at Rouen. Years later a second church inquiry declared the trial void, and in time the Church named her a saint. A church court condemned her, and the Church later called her holy. Her careful answer outlasted the court that asked it.
screen: `A PEASANT GIRL BEFORE A CHURCH COURT.` · `A QUESTION WITH ONLY BAD ANSWERS.` · `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.` · `CONDEMNED, THEN DECLARED A SAINT.` · then, large: `MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer one hard question honestly. Before the sit, let a question come that you've been dodging. Am I being fair to my brother? Do I actually want this job? Is this habit hurting me? Don't grab the answer that makes you look good, or the one that condemns you. Sit still a moment. Try Joan's shape: name both possibilities, and stop pretending to know more than you do. If you pray, you can borrow her words, may God put me there. If you don't, just stay with the question without flinching. The bell holds the time.
Joan's trial. The church court at Rouen that questioned Joan of Arc, and the careful reply its record kept: if I am not in God's grace, may God put me there. Today's word.
Your line: may God put me there. Today, when someone asks you a question with no safe answer, slow down, and give the honest one. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: Rita of Cascia (1381–1457)
830.hook: a wife in a violent marriage who became a peacemaker, patron of impossible causes
830.howItsDone: Catholics ask Saint Rita's prayers for situations that seem hopeless, and on her feast some parishes bless roses and give them to the people who come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan's trial, and a reply that turned a trap into a prayer. Your line was may God put me there. What hard question did you answer honestly? Day eight hundred thirty.

A convent in Cascia, in the hills of Umbria, in the dead of winter. A sick nun asks a visiting cousin for something absurd: a rose from the garden of her old home. The cousin goes, expecting snow and bare branches. Tradition says she found one rose in bloom and carried it back. People still bring roses to that nun's shrine. But long before the convent, her life had held harder things than a winter garden: a hard marriage, a murder, and sons sworn to revenge. Today's word is her name: Rita.
screen: `A ROSE IN THE SNOW.` → `ROSES AT HER SHRINE.` → `A HARDER STORY BEHIND IT.`

segments.voice: Start with the marriage. Tradition says Rita hoped to enter a convent as a girl, but was married instead, to a hard and violent man. The stories say she met him with patience and prayer, and that in time he changed. A word of care here. Rita's story is not a reason to stay in danger. The Catholic bishops of the United States have taught plainly that no one is expected to stay in an abusive marriage. Rita is honored for what came next. Next, the feud. Her husband was killed in a vendetta between families. Her sons, the stories say, swore to avenge him. Rita prayed that they would not become killers, and tradition says they died of illness before they could carry it out. Then, the peace. Alone now, Rita asked to join the Augustinian sisters in Cascia. Tradition says they would not take her while the feud still burned. So she made the peace herself, going between the families until they were reconciled, and then the convent opened its door. Finally, the name. People call Rita the patron of impossible causes. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, the angel tells Mary, "no word shall be impossible with God." Rita's life is read as that verse lived out: a blood feud ended by a widow who had every reason to keep it going. The rose in the snow is the small sign. The reconciled families are the real one.
screen: `A HARD MARRIAGE, MET WITH PRAYER.` · `A MURDER, AND SONS SWORN TO REVENGE.` · `A WIDOW MAKES THE PEACE.` · `NO WORD SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE WITH GOD.` · then, large: `IMPOSSIBLE CAUSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one impossible thing. Before the sit, name a situation that looks stuck. A family that won't speak. A diagnosis. A war on the news. A grudge of your own. Don't try to fix it in two minutes. Just set it down in front of you. Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can hold it up with the angel's words, no word shall be impossible with God, or ask Rita's prayers for it. If you don't, hold it with care instead of despair, and notice whether one small step in it belongs to you. The bell holds the time.
Rita. A wife and widow who, tradition says, ended a feud between families and became an Augustinian nun; the patron of impossible causes. Today's word.
Your line: impossible causes. Today, before you write off something that looks stuck, say the angel's words to yourself once: no word shall be impossible with God. Day eight hundred thirty.

831.title: Nicholas of Flüe (1417–1487)
831.hook: a farmer and father who became a hermit and helped keep Switzerland from civil war
831.howItsDone: Catholics in Switzerland honor Brother Klaus as their patron, and pilgrims still walk down into the Ranft gorge to pray at his cell and chapel. A short prayer attributed to him, asking God to take away whatever keeps the one praying from God, is still prayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rita of Cascia, a widow who ended a feud between families. Your line was impossible causes. Did you say the angel's words over something that looked stuck? Day eight hundred thirty-one.

Night, in a narrow gorge in the Swiss mountains. A priest is hurrying down a steep path toward a small cell built against a chapel. Down in the town of Stans, the leaders of the Swiss confederates have been arguing for days, and the talks are falling apart. Some fear the confederates will turn on one another. The priest has come to ask a hermit what to do. The hermit was a farmer, a soldier, a judge and a father before he walked away from his house to live in this gorge. He is still known by a plainer name. Today's word: Nicholas.
screen: `A PRIEST ON A MOUNTAIN PATH.` → `TALKS FALLING APART IN STANS.` → `A HERMIT IN A GORGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the first life. Nicholas was a farmer in central Switzerland, married to Dorothea, and a father. He served as a soldier and sat as a local judge and councilor, and his neighbors trusted him. Next, the hard choice. Later, Nicholas felt called to leave everything and live for God alone. Tradition says he did not go until Dorothea consented. That is not a small detail. The cost fell on her and the children too, and those who honor him honor her. He built a cell in the Ranft gorge, close enough to home that his family could visit. Tradition says he lived there for years taking no food but the Eucharist. People came anyway, for advice. Then, the night at Stans. With the confederates' talks near collapse, the parish priest of Stans went up to Nicholas and carried his counsel back down. The sources don't give his exact words. But the delegates reached an agreement, and the confederation held together. Tradition remembers the hermit's counsel as the turning point. Finally, the name. He is remembered as Brother Klaus, and the Church honors him as patron of Switzerland. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Brother Klaus made peace without an army, an office or a vote. He had prayer, a name for honesty, and the trust of people who no longer trusted each other.
screen: `A FARMER, JUDGE AND FATHER.` · `A HERMIT, WITH DOROTHEA'S CONSENT.` · `COUNSEL CARRIED DOWN TO STANS.` · `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.` · then, large: `BROTHER KLAUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one peace. Before the sit, bring to mind one small rift. Two coworkers who won't look at each other. A sibling you haven't called. A neighbor over a fence. A quarrel inside yourself. Let your breathing slow. Don't plan a speech. Ask instead what one honest, simple step would lower the heat by a single degree. If you pray, you can pray the beatitude, blessed are the peacemakers, or ask Brother Klaus's prayers. If you don't, just hold both sides of the rift with the same care. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas. A Swiss farmer and father who became a hermit, and whose counsel, tradition says, helped the confederates make peace. Today's word.
Your line: Brother Klaus. Today, be one quiet go-between: carry a kind word from one person to another who have stopped speaking. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: Catherine of Genoa
832.hook: a noblewoman who ran a hospital and taught that purgatory is love's fire
832.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead, especially at Mass and in November, trusting that those being purified are helped by the prayers of the living; Catherine's writing on purgatory is still read as spiritual reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas of Flüe, the hermit whose counsel helped keep the peace. Your line was Brother Klaus. Whose quiet go-between were you? Day eight hundred thirty-two.

She was born into a powerful family of Genoa, and she spends her days changing bandages on a hospital ward. Under her apron, the cloth is fine. She also runs the place: the accounts, the supplies, the staff. When sickness sweeps through Genoa, she stays. Years before, she had been an unhappy young wife who could barely get out of bed. Then something happened to her in a confessional, and it gave her an unexpected way of talking about purgatory. Today's name: Catherine of Genoa.
screen: `A NOBLEWOMAN CHANGING BANDAGES.` → `SHE RUNS THE HOSPITAL.` → `ONCE, AN UNHAPPY YOUNG WIFE.`

segments.voice: Start with the long dark stretch. Catherine was married young to Giuliano Adorno, and the marriage was unhappy; he was careless with money and with her. For years, the stories say, she lived in deep sadness. Next, the turn. Kneeling for confession, tradition says, she was overwhelmed by a sense of God's love so strong she could hardly speak. She left changed. In time Giuliano changed too, and the two of them gave themselves to the sick at the Pammatone hospital in Genoa, where Catherine came to run the house. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says, "sick, and you visited me." Catherine took that at its word. Then, her teaching. Her followers gathered what she said about purgatory, and her picture is not a prison. The Catechism calls purgatory a final purification for those who die in God's grace but still need to be made clean. Catherine describes it from the inside. The soul sees God's love clearly and wants nothing else, and the fire it feels is that love burning away whatever still stands in between. The souls there, she says, suffer and are glad at the same time, because they know where they are going. Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims, that such a person "shall be saved, yet so as by fire." Finally, her own life. Some readers see her teaching written in it first: years of grief, then love burning through, leaving her free to wash other people's wounds.
screen: `A LONG, UNHAPPY MARRIAGE.` · `A CONFESSION, AND A FLOOD OF LOVE.` · `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.` · `PURGATORY AS LOVE'S FIRE.` · then, large: `LOVE BURNS CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone sick, starting from here. Before the sit, bring to mind one person who is ill or worn down: in a hospital, at home, maybe in your own house. Settle, and breathe. See them clearly, their room, their face. Then choose one small, concrete thing you could do for them today. A meal left at the door. A call. A card. An hour sitting with them. A chore done without being asked. If you pray, you can hold them before God, or ask Catherine's prayers. If you don't, just hold them, and settle on the plan. The bell holds the time.
Purgatorium. The Church's name for the final purification of a soul already in God's grace, which Catherine of Genoa pictured as love's own burning. Today's word.
Your line: love burns clean. Today, do the one thing you chose for someone sick, and let it cost you a little time. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

833.title: The printing press (c. 1455)
833.hook: Gutenberg's first great book is the Bible
833.howItsDone: Catholics read printed Scripture at Mass from the lectionary and the Book of the Gospels, and some keep a printed Bible, missal or prayer book at home for daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Genoa, who nursed the sick and called purgatorium love's fire. Your line was love burns clean. What did it cost you to show up for someone sick? Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Ink and oil: that's the smell of this workshop in Mainz. A man leans on the bar of a wooden press, and a sheet comes up wet with black letters in neat columns. Then another sheet, with the same letters in the same places. Then another. Until now, in Europe, a Bible came into the world by a scribe's long labor, one letter at a time. Here the same page is coming off a machine, again and again. The man in charge is Johannes Gutenberg, and the book on his press is the Bible. Today: the printing press.
screen: `INK AND OIL IN MAINZ.` → `THE SAME PAGE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THE BOOK ON THE PRESS: THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Start with the trick. Gutenberg's press used movable type: small metal letters, cast so they could be set into lines, inked, pressed, then taken apart and used again. Next, the book he chose. The great book from his workshop was the Bible in Latin, the Vulgate, the translation the Church read at Mass. It was printed in dark, handsome letters made to look like a scribe's best work. Often the colored initials and decorations were added by hand afterward, so no two copies looked quite alike. Then, what changed. A text copied by hand could drift a little with each copy. A printed page stayed the same from one copy to the next. More people could own books, compare them, and read for themselves. In the years ahead, Catholics and Protestants alike would put presses to work, and that story is coming. Finally, the reason for thanks. The psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Before Mainz, in Europe, that lamp was copied by hand. Now a machine could make it page after page, for many more hands. Your line today calls it the first book printed. That's how the story is sometimes told. Historians would add that printing is older than Gutenberg, and that his Bible is the great book his press is remembered for.
screen: `MOVABLE METAL TYPE.` · `THE BIBLE IN LATIN, THE VULGATE.` · `THE SAME PAGE IN EVERY COPY.` · `THY WORD IS A LAMP TO MY FEET.` · then, large: `THE FIRST BOOK PRINTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for the printed word. Before the sit, reach for one printed thing near you: a Bible, a missal, a prayer card, a novel, a cookbook with someone's notes in the margin. Hold it, and feel its weight. Think of the hands behind it: the writer, the translator, the typesetter, the printer, the person who gave it to you. If you pray, you can thank God for each of them, or pray the psalm's line, thy word is a lamp to my feet. If you don't, just thank them, one by one, in your head. The bell holds the time.
Gutenberg. The craftsman in Mainz whose movable metal type printed the Latin Bible again and again, the same from one copy to the next. Today's word.

Your line: the first book printed. Today, read one printed page slowly, as if someone had copied it by hand for you. And look back on the week: Bridget, the Modern Devotion, Joan, Rita, Brother Klaus, purgatorium, and the press. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

fork.reveal: Gutenberg's great book was the Bible in Latin, the Vulgate, set in letters made to look like a scribe's best hand.

original.note: Latin: the Bible, the great book Gutenberg's press is remembered for.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gutenberg invented printing.
what it means: his press used movable metal type, and the great book it's remembered for is the Bible in Latin.
what a scholar hears: printing is older than Mainz; what his workshop made possible was the same page, copy after copy, with the Vulgate as its great book.
